taxonomic_note: Current Kew/POWO accepted species concept. Historical Verbena combinations remain useful search aliases in sources.
look_here_first: START WITH A MATURE LEAF, not flower color. On a LOW, hairy, spreading Glandularia look for opposite leaves with SMALL BROAD, often fan-shaped major lobes (usually 3–6 pairs), sometimes subdivided, but less finely fernlike than G. bipinnatifida. Next compare the crowded terminal flowering spike and examine an OLD spike: in G. pumila its axis stays comparatively SHORT and COMPACT in fruit. Flowers are small, pale pink-purple to violet, each a single fused tube opening into five lobes. A 10× lens helps find the narrow bract below each hairy ribbed calyx. Check these characters together; either leaf size or purple flowers alone is insufficient.

project_inclusion.range_basis: South-central Texas floristic voucher set explicitly records G. pumila in Uvalde, Medina, and Real counties; Travis and Williamson are also independently documented.
project_inclusion.range_guardrail: Exact county voucher evidence; no inferred counties.

best_field_traits: Low short-lived ANNUAL, often spreading/prostrate or ascending to ~19 cm tall in Williamson County records; heights overlap other species.
Opposite decussate leaves on slender sometimes four-angled, densely hairy stems.
Mature SIMPLE leaf blade often 12–27 mm overall, broadly ovate to triangular, with 3–6 pairs of broader fanlike primary lobes and some second-order cuts.
Both ordinary stiff hairs and tiny STALKED GLANDULAR hairs, sometimes reddish-tipped, especially young shoots and flower parts.
Tight terminal flowering spike with crowded small pink/lilac-purple tubular corollas.
Corolla made of one fused tube with FIVE spreading lobes; often whitish center, NOT five separate petals.
Individual narrow bract immediately SUBTENDS each flower's hairy 5-ribbed calyx; distinguish the two only on a clearly exposed side macro.
Small compact fruiting spike whose axis does NOT elongate greatly, contrasting older elongated G. bipinnatifida spikes.
Use mature foliage, floral tube/calyx and mature fruiting axis TOGETHER; neither flower color nor habit alone confirms species.
morphology_keys.comparison_training: G. bipinnatifida has larger, more deeply and finely 1–2-pinnately dissected leaves and generally a coarser, more feathery appearance. G. pumila is the smaller, compact, broad-lobed plant.
morphology_keys.habit: Small annual, commonly low/spreading or ascending, in Williamson County specimens up to ~19 cm; stems square/4-angled, often hairy with stalked glandular hairs.
morphology_keys.leaf_arrangement: Opposite/decussate SIMPLE leaves, usually petiolate, at nodes on four-sided stems; pair appears at matching heights.
morphology_keys.leaf_dissected: Mid-stem mature leaves often 12–27 mm, outline broadly ovate/triangular. Typically 3–6 pairs of relatively broad, fanlike major lobes with 1–2 further notches; overall less finely/regularly pinnate than most mature G. bipinnatifida. Juvenile leaves and plant vigor vary substantially.
morphology_keys.flowering_structure: Short, tight terminal spike densely filled with individual flowers. One flower per narrow subtending bract; old fruiting axis grows little rather than stretching into obvious separated calyx intervals.
morphology_keys.flower_measurements: Flower limb about 7–8 mm across (UT Williamson); Flower corolla tube ~4–5 mm plus throat ~2–3 mm; North Central Texas key gives corolla tube roughly 8–10 mm depending on measurement convention. Do not mix tube-only and tube-plus-throat numbers.
morphology_keys.fruit: Four dry one-seeded nutlets form inside each persistent 5-toothed calyx; *G. pumila* older fruiting axis remains tightly packed. Field proof requires side-by-side old/young heads, not buds misidentified as mature fruits.
field_checks: Photograph two fully mature opposite leaves, with one complete leaf outlined, at a node.
Macro front view one individual small five-lobed flower; check a short crowded terminal head.
Side macro of stalk and hairy calyx: if separate bract is not clear, label only visible hair/calyx.
Compare mature fruiting spike (preferably post-flowering) with typical G. bipinnatifida to check whether calyces spread out along elongated axis.
If flowers are gone, keep Glandularia cf. pumila unless vegetative anatomy is unusually convincing; do not assume based only on small size.
morphology_keys.stem: Short, low, square/4-angled and mostly green; stalked glandular and nonglandular radiating hairs. Lateral shoots may lie flat, with leaves mostly facing upward.
morphology_keys.calyx_and_bract: Each flower's hairy, gland-bearing 5-ribbed calyx is around 6–6.5 mm in a Williamson County account, with five short unequal tooth tips; the narrow subtending bract is around 5–6 mm, usually a little SHORTER than the calyx. The bract is separate from calyx and sits BELOW it at the spike axis. A hand-held side macro must show attachment before arrow-labeling each.
morphology_keys.glandular_hairs: Stems, leaves and calyces can have a mixture of long nonglandular spreading hairs and shorter stalked glandular hairs with minute terminal heads, reddish in aging material. A normal whole-plant photo does not prove glands are visible.
morphology_keys.flower_anatomy: One fused corolla tube ending in five unequal spreading lobes; flower appearance 5-petaled but technically 5 LOBES. Small compared with G. bipinnatifida; North Central Texas key uses limb ~3–5 mm and tube ~8–10 mm, while detailed Williamson County account reports flower across about 7–8 mm and divides tube/throat segments differently. Do NOT mix tube-only, tube-plus-throat and total flared-limb dimensions.
morphology_keys.habitat: Sunny open prairie, disturbed limestone/clay/caliche openings and shallow dry ground. Exact county voucher evidence already recorded; do not extrapolate Hays County from other known counties.
morphology_keys.crew_rule: SMALL broader-lobed mature leaf + TINY crowded flowers + non-elongating old fruiting spike = strong low-verbena ID. Finer twice-cut fernlike mature leaf + old spike that elongates = prairie verbena. Do not separate using purple versus pink.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Against G. bipinnatifida, G. pumila commonly has a much SMALLER broadly cut/fanlobed mature leaf, a relatively SMALL corolla and a mature fruiting spike that stays SHORT. In G. bipinnatifida typical adult leaves are more feathery and twice-cut, the flowers larger and OLD fruiting spikes lengthen. Both may have hair and overlap in stem length, purple flower color and broad leaf appearance: use 2+ confirmed diagnostic structures.

cross_genus_lookalikes.difference: Both can be low, hairy, and pink/purple flowering; V. canescens has gray canescent foliage and more slender flower spikes, rather than a dense compact Glandularia head and broad fan-lobed leaf.

V. halei often has very deeply divided lower leaves but narrow upper leaves and elongate slender spikes, whereas G. pumila is a low compact plant with small broadly lobed leaves and a short persistent head.

crew_key: 1. OPPOSITE leaves? Very small LOW plant? Continue, not proof.
2. Mature leaf is BROAD with 3–6 paired fan-shaped lobes, and secondary NOTCHES but usually not a deeply feathery blade? Supports pumila.
3. Check a true 5-lobed tubular corolla and compact flowering spike; not five independent petals.
4. On side macro identify the calyx and any visible gland-headed hairs, without mistaking the separate bract for a calyx tooth.
5. Find an OLD mature spike; if it remains densely compact, it supports pumila. Strongly elongated spike with spaced old calyces favors bipinnatifida.
6. If G. bipinnatifida remains plausible, enter Glandularia sp. / uncertain pending mature leaf + fruit-head photos.
comparisons.caution: A matched mature leaf photograph and older spike are much more discriminative than one blossom. Both species are genuinely native within the target region. Avoid pulling either as a weed based on rough ID.

visual_comparison.title: Low verbena — verified diagnostic structures
visual_comparison.subtitle: Real photos of the exact species: leaf lobes, small five-lobed corolla, crowded buds and hairy calyces. No mature fruit-spike or separated bract anatomy is asserted.

items.label: Fan-lobed leaf and small flowers
items.image_role: One broad, deeply cut SIMPLE leaf and tiny individual pink-purple corollas visible together
items.caption: The upper broad green blade is ONE deeply lobed leaf rather than separate leaflets. At lower right, tiny pink corollas and crowded green floral parts form one terminal flowering spike, NOT ripe fruit.
items.why_it_matters: Leaf size and major lobe shape matter more than pink versus purple color. A photographed flowering head does not prove the compact mature fruiting condition.

items.label: Mature leaves, complete flower and compact flowering spike
items.image_role: Leaf with broad toothed/secondary lobes, one five-lobed fused corolla, and a compact flower-bud cluster
items.caption: An entire simple blade has broad lobes and additional notches; one purple flower is a fused tubular corolla with five outward lobes; the nearby round group is still FLOWERING and budding, not a confirmed old fruiting spike.
items.why_it_matters: Demonstrates the primary vegetative identification clue and prevents confusion between unopened floral buds and mature fruit.

items.label: Hairy individual calyces and floral stalk
items.image_role: Side macro of hairy, ribbed calyx tubes and projecting stem hairs
items.caption: The green/purplish small tubular flower coverings are hairy calyces; the flower-stalk surface carries conspicuous projecting hairs. Tiny gland heads versus simple hairs and any single separate subtending bract cannot be isolated confidently in this photo.
items.why_it_matters: Shows the true scale and hairy flower architecture without labeling a bract or tiny glands that the pixels cannot distinguish.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Low verbena: compare the LEAF before the flowers
steps: Find a mature BROAD, fan-lobed simple leaf; its notches do not make it compound.
Check a little five-lobed fused tubular flower and short crowded flowering head.
On the side view look for tiny hairy floral calyces; tiny gland heads and bracts still need a sharper macro.
Then compare a genuinely OLD fruiting spike against prairie verbena before finalizing difficult IDs.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: Low + small, broadly lobed mature leaves + little flowers + compact OLD fruiting spike together strongly support G. pumila. Never decide from flower color alone.
field_photo_quickcheck.warning: The pictured flower heads include buds, not confirmed fully ripe spikes. Exact gland heads, individual subtending bract and mature four-nutlet fruit remain unmarked until better images are found.
